tier_reason: README 性能对比 table gives first-party run times vs Boost for add/sub/mul/div/modexp at 256-4096 bits, but no benchmark source is in the repo (UnitTest/ and example/ hold only tests and a demo), and no compiler flags, CPU model, Boost version/backend or units are stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (run time, lower is better; 500,000 ops for add/sub/mul/div, 1,000 for modexp), Unsigned Bigint vs boost: multiply 0.019142 vs 0.0335125 at 256 bits and 1.2972828 vs 5.5994093 at 4096 bits (1.75x to 4.32x across sizes, derived from page data); modular exponentiation 0.0675292 vs 0.2627964 at 256 bits and 52.701681 vs 445.34939 at 4096 bits (3.9x and 8.4x; peak 10.3x at 2048 bits, 7.361546 vs 76.14449; derived from page data); add 1.4x to 2.6x and subtract 1.5x to 3.0x faster (derived from page data). Division is slower at every size: 0.9787682 vs 0.2175322 at 256 bits (about 4.5x slower) and 11.174972 vs 10.216111 at 4096 bits.
corrections.caveats: First-party table without benchmark source in the repository, compiler flags, CPU model, Boost version or backend (cpp_int fixed or dynamic), or run-time units. Division loses to Boost at every size shown (4.5x slower at 256 bits). Repository has a single commit ('first commit', 2019-06-01), Visual Studio 2017 solution only with MASM assembly, so effectively Windows/MSVC-only and abandoned. Not compared against GMP.

notes: README numbers match the record; the add/subtract range in the record (1.4x-2.4x) was understated and is corrected from the table. Only one commit exists (2019-06-01), so maintenance is abandoned.

tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (benchmark/bench_fft.cpp, bench_nd.cpp, bench_harness.hpp; FFTW arm plans once with FFTW_MEASURE outside the timed loop), and benchmark/README.md states GCC 14.2, Xeon w5-3435X and the release preset, whose flags (Release, -march=native, -ffast-math by default) are public in CMakePresets.json and docs/build-options.md. Only pooled ratios are published, not per-size times, and the run is the author's own.

corrections.baseline: FFTW 3 (FFTW_MEASURE, single thread; version and build flags of the system fftw3 not stated in the admiral repo, while the author's separate fft_bench uses FFTW 3.3.11); also ducc0 (commit c4dda23)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, CMake 'release' preset: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's GCC default -O3 -DNDEBUG), ADM_TARGET_ARCH=native (-march=native), ADM_USE_FAST_MATH=ON (-ffast-math, the default), LTO off; sweep of 2026-08-24 per benchmark/README.md. FFTW is the system fftw3/fftw3f found via pkg-config, configure flags not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks, 188 commits (oldest commit on the first commits page 2026-09-11; the README sweep is dated 2026-08-24, so the history goes back further)
corrections.caveats: Benchmark is run by the library author, and the same author (DiamonDinoia) wrote the fft_bench shootout repo, so that repo is not independent evidence. Only pooled ratios are published (FFTW: 19 1-D lengths and 9 N-D shapes, both precisions pooled), no per-size times. Admiral is built with -ffast-math by default (relaxed IEEE, flushed denormals), though every timed size is accuracy-gated against a reference DFT; FFTW's version and build flags (e.g. whether AVX-512 codelets were enabled) are not stated for the w5-3435X sweep. In bench_fft.cpp the 1-D ducc0 arm calls ducc0_forward_fft, which allocates and zero-fills a fresh output std::vector inside the timed lambda while Admiral reuses a preallocated buffer, so the 1-D ducc0 ratios (2.18x/2.70x) carry allocation overhead that matters most at small N; the N-D ducc0 arm and the FFTW arm use preallocated buffers. In the fft_bench plots (images only) Admiral is roughly tied with MKL and FFTW over much of the 1-D range single-threaded on Xeon Platinum 8362 and EPYC 9474F, with MKL ahead at small sizes on Intel, FFTW ahead at small sizes on AMD, Sleef ahead at mid and large sizes on EPYC 9474F, and multi-threaded MKL clearly ahead for large 1-D on the Intel node; that README marks its MKL-omp numbers for rome and genoa as invalid. 16-thread 1-D vs threaded ducc0 is mixed per benchmark/README.md (geomean 0.33x to 1.82x by size). Very new project; the README says much of the code and cost-model tuning was done with Claude and that the author does not claim the fastest FFT. License is BSD-3-Clause-Attribution (adds an acknowledgment clause naming the Admiral FFT library), which the SPDX license list marks as not OSI-approved, hence usability reference.

notes: All headline numbers match README.md and benchmark/README.md. Usability changed to reference because BSD-3-Clause-Attribution is not OSI-approved (SPDX license-list-data 3.29.0: isOsiApproved false). fft_bench is by the same owner (DiamonDinoia) and lists Admiral at commit b2bf2d3, so it adds plots but no independence; I viewed three of its plots (1-D ST icelake and genoa, 1-D MT icelake) and they match the record's description.

tier_reason: Code for both baselines is public: M1 GPU kernels with src/fft_host.swift and the vDSP baseline in benchmarks/Sources/vdsp_baseline_bench.swift (swiftc -O, Apple M1), and for M6 the M6Bench harness plus m6/benchmarks/micro/sme/sme_stage5.c built with clang -O3 -mcpu=apple-m4 on an Apple M6 under macOS 27.0, with raw logs in m6/results whose headers record date, OS and build line. Toolchain versions are not stated for the M1 run, which is the weaker half.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Apple M1, N=4096 batch=256 (README): radix-8 Stockham 138.45 GFLOPS (1.78 us/FFT) vs vDSP 107.0 GFLOPS (2.29 us/FFT), +29%; in-place Cooley-Tukey with simdgroup_matrix 128 GFLOPS (+20%); radix-4 Stockham 113.6 GFLOPS (+6%). Apple M6 (m6/README.md): one-pass N=8192/16384 kernels 2.2x / 1.85x faster than MPSGraph (4.4x with FP16 storage); per m6/results/stage3_onepass.stdout this holds at DRAM-resident batches (N=8192 batch 2048: 604.4 vs 257.4 GF hot; N=16384 batch 1024: 547.2 vs 296.0 GF cold), while at L2-resident N=16384 MPSGraph is faster (805.2 vs 220.4 GF). CPU SME2 radix-8 FFT 'up to 5.3x' vDSP is the column-FFT case (m6/results/stage5_col.stdout, N=512 x W=256 matrix, 1 thread: SME 263.4 GF vs vDSP transpose+fftm+transpose 49.6 GF); for contiguous batched FFTs (stage5_fft.stdout) SME-CG beats vDSP_fft by 1.21x to 3.52x, but only 0.51x to 1.76x once packing into the SME layout is counted, i.e. slower than vDSP at N>=512.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: M1: xcrun metal + metallib; host swiftc -O -framework Metal -framework Accelerate (Xcode and macOS versions not stated). M6: swift build -c release for the M6Bench harness; SME2 C kernels clang -O3 -mcpu=apple-m4 (build line recorded in each m6/results log header).
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 (main README; GPU core count and macOS version not stated); Apple M6, macOS 27.0 (m6/README.md; logs dated 2026-09-26)
corrections.caveats: The M1 +29% compares the whole GPU against a single CPU core: GPU kernels are timed from the command buffer's gpuStartTime to gpuEndTime (GPU execution only, dispatch overhead excluded), while the vDSP baseline (benchmarks/Sources/vdsp_baseline_bench.swift) is one thread looping vDSP_fft_zop (radix-2 setup, split complex) and timing the wall clock; a multithreaded vDSP baseline was not measured. The M1 headline is for one size (N=4096, batch 256); the multi-size table (N=256 to 16384, batch 64) lists GFLOPS without vDSP columns. On M6 the one-pass kernels beat MPSGraph only at DRAM-resident batches (MPSGraph is 3.7x faster at L2-resident N=16384, derived from page data), and the SME2 'up to 5.3x' figure is for column FFTs of a matrix; for contiguous batches with packing counted the SME path is slower than vDSP at N>=512. Hot and cold runs differ by up to 3.7x per the m6 README. The M6 hardware and macOS 27.0 may be hard for a verifier to reproduce. Research code (Metal kernels, Swift host harnesses, C SME2 kernels), not a packaged C++ library. Results come from the author's own preprints (arXiv 2603.27569 for the M1 paper and 2609.32237 for the M6 paper per search results), not peer reviewed as far as could be checked. Baseline is Apple-specific (vDSP, MPSGraph), not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT.

notes: README numbers match. The vDSP baseline is a single-threaded loop and GPU time is GPU-only, so the +29% is GPU vs one CPU core; the SME2 5.3x is the matrix-column case and the SME path loses to vDSP on contiguous batches once packing is included. arxiv.org is blocked here, so the arXiv IDs come from a WebSearch result only.
